title: Measurement Conversion Worksheets
intro: The quantity stays the same when its unit changes. Count how many smaller units make each larger unit.
html:
Smaller units give a larger count

A length of three meters can also be described as 300 centimeters. The length has not grown: centimeters are smaller, so more of them are needed to measure the same length.

1 meter = 100 centimeters
1 kilogram = 1000 grams
1 liter = 1000 milliliters
1 foot = 12 inches

Multiply by the number of smaller units

For 3 meters, count three groups of 100 centimeters: 3 × 100 = 300. For 4 kilograms, count four groups of 1000 grams: 4 × 1000 = 4000. Write the requested unit beside the result.

Keep the kind of measurement

Meters and centimeters describe length. Kilograms and grams describe mass. Liters and milliliters describe volume. Knowing that one kilogram is 1000 grams does not mean one kilogram equals 1000 milliliters; those measure different things.

Feet and inches use a different relationship

One foot is 12 inches. Five feet is 5 × 12 = 60 inches. Do not use 100 or 1000 just because those factors work for the metric pairs on this sheet.

If the child divides when changing to smaller units: imagine measuring the same length with shorter pieces. More pieces are needed. Return to one larger unit, name how many smaller units it contains, then multiply by the given amount.

Check by grouping back

If 6 liters becomes 6000 milliliters, grouping 6000 milliliters into groups of 1000 should recover 6 liters. For 84 inches, groups of 12 recover 7 feet. This inverse check supports the conversion even though the worksheet asks only for the smaller unit.

About this practice

Each sheet reuses four original questions, one for each relationship above. Starting amounts are whole numbers from 2 through 9. Metric conversions stay within the metric system; feet to inches stays within the customary system.

This sheet does not convert between metric and customary systems, use decimal or mixed-unit amounts, or ask for reverse conversions. It covers selected relationships rather than all measurement units.
